0.title: All Is Vanity — and Yet
0.overview:
Ecclesiastes is the most daring book in Scripture. The Preacher — Qohelet in Hebrew, the Assembler, the one who gathers wisdom and weighs experience — opens not with a doxology but with a diagnosis: hebel. The word is usually translated “vanity,” but it means literally “breath” or “vapor.” Mist. It appears thirty-eight times in twelve chapters. The Preacher is not being melodramatic. He is being precise.

What is hebel? It is the quality of things that look solid but dissolve when grasped. Not evil — vaporous. Not sinful — ephemeral. The river runs to the sea and the sea is never full. The sun rises and the sun sets. Generations come and go and the earth endures indifferent. You pour your life into work and a stranger inherits it. You accumulate wisdom and die alongside the fool. This is not despair; it is diagnosis. Under the sun, without God, this is what is simply and factually true.

Timothy Keller often observed that Ecclesiastes is the most postmodern book in the Bible because it takes the secular experience with total seriousness. The Preacher does not argue against life without God from the outside — he grants the premise and follows it ruthlessly to its conclusion. Pleasure (chapter 2). Wealth and great projects (chapter 2). Wisdom itself (chapter 1). Justice perverted (chapter 3). Loneliness (chapter 4). Religious performance without heart (chapter 5). Each time, the verdict is the same: vanity, and a striving after wind.

But Ecclesiastes is not the counsel of despair. It is a diagnostic instrument wielded by a faithful God to prepare his people for good news. The path from vanity to meaning runs straight through the cross and out the other side. Jesus Christ, the eternal Son, entered fully into hebel. He was born of a woman, born under the law, born into the cycles of toil and grief and death the Preacher catalogues. He asked the Preacher’s ultimate question from the cross: My God, my God, why? And God answered from the empty tomb. The resurrection is God’s answer to every chapter of Ecclesiastes. There is work that is not in vain in the Lord (1 Cor. 15:58). There is an inheritance that does not perish (1 Pet. 1:4). There is a joy no one can take away (John 16:22). There is a wisdom that is not a striving after wind — it is Christ himself, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2:3).

Read Ecclesiastes slowly. Let it expose every substitute saviour you have been carrying. Let the weight of hebel press on you until you feel how hollow life is without God. And then hear the gospel again — not as a comfortable habit, but as the only answer to a question Qohelet spent twelve chapters asking.

1.title: Ecclesiastes 1 — Vanity of Vanities: The Opening Verdict

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Life Under the Sun: The Problem Stated
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Preacher opens with the book's controlling verdict—hebel, vanity, vapor—and immediately grounds it in observation: the cycles of nature (sun, wind, streams) are tireless but lead nowhere. Human labor is ceaseless but gains nothing permanent. Wisdom itself, pursued with all the passion Qohelet can muster, only deepens the pain. The opening chapter does not offer resolution; it poses the question that the whole book will wrestle with.
verseByVerse.theology: The word hebel (vapor, breath, vanity) occurs 38 times in Ecclesiastes. It describes something real but insubstantial—a morning mist, a breath of air, here and then gone. Qohelet uses it to describe not that life is meaningless but that it is ungraspable: it cannot be seized, secured, or leveraged into lasting significance by human effort alone. The phrase 'under the sun' (28 occurrences) marks the perspective: life viewed from the horizontal, from within the created order, without the vertical revelation of God's eternal purpose. The answer to hebel is not despair but the fear of God—which is why the book must diagnose the disease before it can prescribe the cure.
verseByVerse.examples: Kidner: 'Qohelet is not a pessimist; he is a ruthless realist.' The opening cycles of sun, wind, and water are not depressing observations about futility but a rigorous epistemology: if you are looking for gain from the created order alone, you are looking in the wrong direction. Keller notes that Ecclesiastes is the most contemporary book in the Bible—its diagnosis of what happens when humans seek ultimate meaning in finite things describes every secular culture exactly.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The superscription locates the book in wisdom tradition: 'the son of David, king in Jerusalem' points to Solomon, the wisest of Israel's kings (1 Kgs 3–4; 10). The term 'Preacher' renders the Hebrew Qohelet—one who addresses an assembly, a convener of wisdom. The title establishes authority: this is not the musing of an ordinary person but the considered verdict of the one uniquely positioned to test all of life's possibilities. Whatever wisdom, wealth, pleasure, and power can offer—Solomon had it. His verdict therefore carries maximum weight.

verseByVerse.quote: Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities! All is vanity. What does man gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Vanity of vanities'—the Hebrew superlative form (like 'Song of Songs' or 'Holy of Holies'), meaning the most absolute, concentrated hebel imaginable. From the first breath the Preacher refuses false comfort. He will not begin with what we wish were true; he begins with what he has actually observed. The question of verse 3—'What does man gain?'—uses the commercial word for profit (yitron). The Preacher is asking: at the end of all human striving, what is the net return? His answer, demonstrated throughout the book, is: nothing that lasts. Kidner: 'A doctor who lies about a diagnosis does not love his patient. The Preacher loves us enough to tell the truth.'

verseByVerse.quote: A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever. The sun rises, and the sun goes down, and hastens to its place where it rises. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The first cycle: human generations pass but the earth persists—a haunting reversal of expectations. We feel like we should be permanent; the earth should be the transient thing. But it is the reverse. Then the sun: rising and setting, 'hastening' back to its starting point—the image of exhausted, purposeless motion. The sun works harder than any human laborer, yet arrives back where it started every morning. Its ceaseless activity produces no progress. This is the world as Qohelet observes it from beneath: energetic, beautiful, and circular.

verseByVerse.quote: The wind blows to the south and goes around to the north; around and around goes the wind, and on its circuits the wind returns. All streams run to the sea, but the sea is not full; to the place where the streams flow, there they flow again. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Wind and water: both work ceaselessly and both return to their origins. The wind circles; the rivers pour into the sea—yet the sea never fills. The water cycle (evaporation, cloud, rain, river) is perfectly described: the rivers flow to the sea, rise again as vapor, fall as rain, and flow again. But Qohelet's point is not meteorological; it is existential. All this energy produces no accumulation, no advance, no gain. The created order is beautiful and ingenious, but it does not improve. This is the world without God at its center—magnificent and going nowhere.

verseByVerse.quote: All things are full of weariness; a man cannot utter it; the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing. What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The created order's ceaseless motion is wearisome—not boring but exhausting in the way a treadmill exhausts: much effort, no destination. The eye and ear are never satisfied—human desire is infinite but the supply is finite. This is not cynicism but anthropology: we are made for more than this world can give. 'Nothing new under the sun'—history repeats its patterns. Wars, empires, technologies, philosophies—they cycle like the wind. Waltke: 'The absence of the new is not mere observation but a theological statement: genuine newness can only come from outside the system.'

verseByVerse.quote: Is there a thing of which it is said, 'See, this is new'? It has been already in the ages before us. There is no remembrance of former things, nor will there be any remembrance of things that are to come among those who come after. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Is there a thing of which it is said, See, this is new?'—Qohelet anticipates the objection. The things we call new are only new to us because we have forgotten the old. And we too will be forgotten. This is one of the most sobering verses in the Bible: the forgetting is universal and inevitable. The greatest achievements of the greatest people are eventually swallowed by time. Keller: 'The library of time erases its own books.' The remedy is not fame-seeking but finding one's name written in the book that does not perish—the Lamb's book of life.

verseByVerse.quote: I the Preacher have been king over Israel in Jerusalem. And I applied my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom all that is done under heaven. It is an unhappy business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Preacher's credentials are restated and the investigation begins. 'Applied my heart'—the Hebrew phrase for total intellectual and volitional engagement. He is not a dilettante; he pursues the question with everything he has. 'It is an unhappy business'—the word for 'unhappy' (ra) is the word for evil or bad; the word for 'business' (inyan) means occupation or preoccupation. The search for ultimate meaning from within creation is, God has arranged, a frustrating preoccupation. God has embedded the frustration to drive us toward himself. This is the pedagogy of Ecclesiastes: pain as teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: I have seen everything that is done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and a striving after wind. What is crooked cannot be made straight, and what is lacking cannot be counted. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Striving after wind'—the Hebrew re'ut ruach can also be translated 'feeding on wind.' Both images capture futility: you cannot catch or eat the wind. 'What is crooked cannot be made straight'—a proverb that states the limits of human power. There is a structural wrongness in the world (theologians call it the Fall) that human ingenuity cannot fix. 'What is lacking cannot be counted'—the deficits are beyond enumeration. Qohelet is not counsel to passivity but to realism: know what human hands can and cannot accomplish before you set your heart on it.

verseByVerse.quote: I said in my heart, 'I have acquired great wisdom, surpassing all who were over Jerusalem before me, and my heart has had great experience of wisdom and knowledge.' And I applied my heart to know wisdom and to know madness and folly. I perceived that this also is but a striving after wind. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Preacher's self-assessment is honest and sweeping: he has more wisdom than any predecessor. He pursues wisdom comprehensively—including madness and folly—to understand the full spectrum. Yet even wisdom, pursued as an end in itself, is hebel. This is the theological heart of the chapter: wisdom is a gift and a tool, but it is not the foundation. When wisdom is made ultimate—when it becomes the source of meaning rather than a means in the service of the fear of God—it fails. Sproul: 'Wisdom without God is the most sophisticated form of vanity.'

verseByVerse.quote: For in much wisdom is much vexation, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The final verse of the chapter is not a reason to avoid wisdom but a description of what wisdom reveals. The more you understand about the human condition—its injustice, its finitude, its cycles of futility—the more it grieves you. A fool is protected from this sorrow by his ignorance. The wise person sees clearly and therefore hurts deeply. This is what drove Qohelet to despair in chapter 2—not stupidity but insight. The answer is not less wisdom but wisdom in its proper place: in subordination to the God who made both the world and the wise person who observes it.

2.title: Ecclesiastes 2 — The Experiment with Pleasure and Work

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — The Great Experiment: Pleasure, Achievement, Wisdom—and Their Verdict
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Having found wisdom alone insufficient, Qohelet turns to pleasure, then to monumental achievement, then to comparative wisdom. He denies himself nothing. He builds, plants, acquires, accumulates with extraordinary energy. At the end he surveys it all and pronounces the same verdict: vanity. Yet the chapter does not end in despair: vv. 24–26 introduce the first of Ecclesiastes' carpe diem refrains—eat, drink, find enjoyment in your toil, for this is from God's hand.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter is a systematic experiment in the Enlightenment project before the Enlightenment: can the human person, through total control of circumstances, manufacture a meaningful and satisfying life? Qohelet's answer is no—not because the things he tries are evil, but because none of them can bear the weight of ultimate meaning. Pleasure is good but cannot satisfy the soul. Achievement is significant but cannot outlast the achiever. Wisdom is better than folly—but the wise man and the fool die the same death. The 'under the sun' perspective consistently produces the same result: the finite cannot fill the infinite appetite of the human heart.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller identifies the structure of vv. 1–11 as the most sophisticated anticipation of modern consumer culture in the ancient world: 'Qohelet tried everything the secular person tries today—pleasure, beauty, achievement, accumulation—and he had resources to pursue them all without limit. His report from inside the experiment is the most valuable data point available.' The carpe diem conclusion (vv. 24–26) is not resignation but wisdom: receive what God gives today as a gift, without demanding that it give you what only God can give.

verseByVerse.quote: I said in my heart, 'Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy yourself.' But behold, this also was vanity. I said of laughter, 'It is mad,' and of pleasure, 'What does it accomplish?' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The experiment begins with deliberate, methodical self-indulgence. 'I will test you with pleasure'—the language is clinical: this is a research project, not an abandonment to passion. The verdict comes before the details: 'this also was vanity.' The preemptive verdict shows that Qohelet is looking back on the experiment, not writing during it. Laughter he calls 'mad'—not sinful but incoherent, disconnected from reality. Pleasure 'accomplishes' nothing permanent. The problem is not that pleasure is bad but that it cannot do what the human heart asks of it.

verseByVerse.quote: I searched with my heart how to cheer my body with wine—my heart still guiding me with wisdom—and how to lay hold on folly, till I might see what was good for the children of man to do under heaven during the few days of their life. I made great works. I built houses and planted vineyards for myself. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'My heart still guiding me with wisdom'—the experiment is controlled: Qohelet does not abandon wisdom while pursuing pleasure; he uses wisdom to maximize pleasure. This is important: the verdict against pleasure is not from someone who failed at it but from someone who mastered it. Then achievement: 'I made great works.' The scale is Solomonic (1 Kgs 7–9)—building programs, vineyards, agricultural projects. This is the ancient equivalent of building an empire: material creation on the largest possible scale.

verseByVerse.quote: I made myself gardens and parks, and planted in them all kinds of fruit trees. I made myself pools from which to water the forest of growing trees. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Gardens, parks, fruit trees, irrigation pools—the Preacher is describing the ancient royal ideal of paradise (the word 'park' is the Persian word for a walled garden, pardes, from which we get 'paradise'). He is not merely gardening; he is re-creating Eden on command. Pools to water forests—the engineering is ambitious. The irony is theological: he is building what only God can create permanently. His paradise is magnificent but it is his—finite, mortal, unable to outlast him.

verseByVerse.quote: I bought male and female slaves, and had slaves who were born in my house. I had also great possessions of herds and flocks, more than any who had been before me in Jerusalem. I also gathered for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces. I got singers, both men and women, and many concubines, the delight of the sons of man. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Human capital, animal capital, financial capital, cultural capital (singers), and erotic capital—each category is maximized. The phrase 'more than any who had been before me in Jerusalem' is the refrain of supremacy: this is the pinnacle achievable by human accumulation. Kidner notes that the list is deliberately comprehensive: Qohelet leaves no category of human desire untested. What remains after total acquisition? The verdict of verse 11: nothing to be gained. The experiment is exhaustive and the result is uniform.

verseByVerse.quote: So I became great and surpassed all who were before me in Jerusalem. Also my wisdom remained with me. And whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them. I kept my heart from no pleasure, for my heart found pleasure in all my toil, and this was my reward for all my toil. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'My wisdom remained with me'—the experiment was conducted at full cognitive capacity; it was not self-deception or drunken excess but clear-eyed accumulation. 'Whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them'—total self-permission, total resource availability. 'This was my reward for all my toil'—he acknowledges that there was a real pleasure in the toil itself. The present enjoyment of work and its fruits is genuine and good. Qohelet will say so again in vv. 24–26. The problem is not the pleasure but the conclusion that the pleasure draws: that it constitutes the meaning of life.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I considered all that my hands had done and the toil I had expended in doing it, and behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The survey moment: Qohelet steps back and examines his entire achievement from the outside. 'Behold'—a word of surprise, of discovery. Even he is surprised by the emptiness at the center of his fullness. 'All was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was nothing to be gained under the sun.' Three consecutive expressions of futility—the triple emphasis is deliberate and devastating. What the greatest accumulation of resources in Jerusalem's history produces: vapor, wind, zero net gain. The experiment is complete and the result is conclusive.

verseByVerse.quote: So I turned to consider wisdom and madness and folly, for what can the man do who comes after the king? Only what has already been done. Then I saw that there is more gain in wisdom than in folly, as there is more gain in light than in darkness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Preacher is fair: he does not conclude that wisdom is useless. 'There is more gain in wisdom than in folly, as there is more gain in light than in darkness'—the comparison is apt and the preference is clear. Walking in daylight is better than stumbling in the dark. Wisdom provides real advantages in navigation, decision-making, relationships. But verse 14 introduces the fatal qualification that undoes the advantage: the same event happens to both. Wisdom's advantage is real but it is not ultimate.

verseByVerse.quote: The wise person has his eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. And yet I perceived that the same event happens to all of them. Then I said in my heart, 'What happens to the fool will happen to me also. Why then have I been so very wise?' And I said in my heart that this also is vanity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The same event happens to all'—death levels the distinction between wisdom and folly. The wise man sees clearly; the fool stumbles; but both arrive at the same destination. Qohelet's pain is not abstract: 'Why then have I been so very wise?' If wisdom and folly both end in the grave, wisdom's advantage is temporary. This is not the whole truth—Qohelet knows there is a God who judges (3:17), and Proverbs knows that wisdom has eternal foundations. But under the sun, in the horizontal, the leveling is real and must be faced honestly.

verseByVerse.quote: For there is no remembrance of the wise more than of the fool forever, since in the days to come all will have been long forgotten. How the wise dies just like the fool! So I hated life, because what is done under the sun was grievous to me, for all is vanity and a striving after wind. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I hated life'—the low point of the chapter. This is not clinical despair but the honest reaction of a man who has done everything right and found it insufficient. The wise die forgotten just like the fools. The radical equality of the grave removes the last advantage wisdom seemed to offer. Qohelet does not resolve this pain immediately—the book allows it to sit and ache. This is pastorally important: Ecclesiastes does not rush past the reality of human grief. Keller: 'The man who says he hates life is a man who loved life and found it unable to hold his love.'

verseByVerse.quote: I hated all my toil in which I toil under the sun, seeing that I must leave it to the man who comes after me, and who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will be master of all for which I toiled and used my wisdom under the sun. This also is vanity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The heir problem: everything built with wisdom will be inherited by someone of unknown character. The successor might be a fool. He might squander what wisdom built. This is not a minor inconvenience but a structural problem with legacy-building as a meaning-strategy: you cannot control what happens to your work after you die. Every person who has built something significant and then aged has felt this. The Preacher names it: this also is vanity. We cannot secure our achievements beyond our lifetimes.

verseByVerse.quote: So I turned about and gave my heart up to despair over all the toil of my labors under the sun, because sometimes a person who has toiled with wisdom and knowledge and skill must leave everything to be enjoyed by someone who did not toil for it. This also is vanity and a great evil. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Gave my heart up to despair'—the Hebrew word (ya'ash) is strong: abandonment, hopelessness. Qohelet does not paper over the emotional consequence of his conclusions. The injustice is pointed: the one who toiled with wisdom and knowledge and skill—three terms emphasizing genuine effort and competence—leaves everything to someone who contributed nothing. Kidner: 'This is the economy of grace applied in the wrong direction—the inheritance going to the undeserving not as gift but as brute accident.' The great evil is the structural unfairness of the system.

verseByVerse.quote: What has a man from all the toil and striving of heart with which he toils beneath the sun? For all his days are full of sorrow, and his work is a grief; even in the night his heart does not rest. This also is vanity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Even in the night his heart does not rest'—the driven achiever carries his work to bed. The anxiety of ambition does not clock out. This is a recognizable portrait of the person who has made achievement the center of their identity: the sorrow that pervades their days and the restlessness that invades their nights. The word 'striving' (inyan) is the same as the 'unhappy business' of 1:13: God has arranged the world so that life without him at the center produces precisely this ceaseless, fruitless labor.

verseByVerse.quote: There is nothing better for a person than that he should eat and drink and find enjoyment in his toil. This also, I saw, is from the hand of God, for apart from him who can eat or who can have enjoyment? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The first of Ecclesiastes' carpe diem refrains—and its theological grounding. 'From the hand of God'—the enjoyment of food, drink, and work is not an escape from reality but a reception of gift. The person who eats with gratitude is practicing theology: acknowledging that the meal comes from God's hand. 'Apart from him who can eat or have enjoyment?'—the rhetorical question affirms that genuine pleasure is not self-generated but God-given. The secular person who eats without gratitude is not fully enjoying the meal; they are missing its deepest dimension.

verseByVerse.quote: For to the one who pleases him God gives wisdom and knowledge and joy, but to the sinner he gives the business of gathering and collecting, only to give to one who pleases God. This also is vanity and a striving after wind. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter ends with a sovereign declaration: God is not absent from this economy. He gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to those who please him—and the sinner's accumulation ends up in the hands of the righteous. This is a foretaste of the eschatological reversal: the meek will inherit the earth (Matt 5:5). The vanity of the sinner's accumulation is not merely existential but judicial—God has arranged the system so that labor without him ultimately serves those who live with him. Sproul: 'The economy of grace is the last word on every economy of works.'

3.title: Ecclesiastes 3 — A Time for Everything: God's Sovereignty and Human Limits

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Poem of Times: God's Governance of All Seasons
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The famous time-poem lists fourteen pairs of contrasting activities, each governed by its proper season. The poem is not fatalistic ('everything happens randomly') but theistic: God has appointed times for everything. The structure is an argument: if every human activity has its appointed time, then the universe is governed by a sovereign purpose, not by chance or chaos.
verseByVerse.theology: The poem's fourteen pairs span the full range of human experience: birth and death, planting and uprooting, killing and healing, building and tearing down, weeping and laughing, mourning and dancing, gathering and scattering stones, embracing and refraining, seeking and losing, keeping and casting away, tearing and mending, silence and speech, love and hate, war and peace. The comprehensiveness is theological: God's governance extends to every domain of human life without exception. Nothing falls outside his appointed order.
verseByVerse.examples: Kidner: 'The poem is not a counsel of passivity but of discernment—the task of the wise is to know which time it is.' The person who mourns when it is time to dance, or dances when it is time to mourn, is out of step with God's governance. Wisdom is the ability to read the times correctly. This is why the poem is followed immediately by the question of verse 9: the governance of times belongs to God; what then does the human worker gain? The answer develops through vv. 10–22.

verseByVerse.quote: For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven: a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up what is planted. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'For everything there is a season'—the Hebrew eth means appointed time, the right moment. The poem begins with the most fundamental pair: birth and death. These are the outer brackets of human existence; everything else happens between them. Neither is in human control—the one who is born did not choose to be born; the one who dies did not (ultimately) choose the day. Then planting and uprooting: the agricultural rhythm that governs all food production. Both are necessary; both have their proper time. The poem is not saying that death is as desirable as birth, but that both belong to God's order.

verseByVerse.quote: A time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up; a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Killing and healing—war and medicine, destruction and restoration. Breaking down and building up—demolition and construction; both are necessary; neither is intrinsically evil. Weeping and laughing—the full emotional range of human experience is included. Mourning and dancing—the Jewish world knew both the sitting of shiva (mourning the dead) and the ecstatic celebration of wedding or victory. God is present in both. Kidner: 'The poem does not flatten human experience into a uniform gray but acknowledges that God governs the full spectrum of what it means to be human.'

verseByVerse.quote: A time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing; a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Casting and gathering stones—perhaps clearing a field or building a wall: both agricultural work and construction require both activities. Embrace and refrain—the full arc of human intimacy: there are times to draw close and times to hold back, times for touch and times for restraint. Seek and lose—sometimes the appointed activity is pursuit; sometimes it is relinquishment. Keep and cast away—the same. The poem is teaching discernment: not everything that is good to do at one time is good to do at all times. Wisdom reads the moment.

verseByVerse.quote: A time to tear, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak; a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Tear and sew—garment repair and garment tearing (as in mourning; cf. Job 1:20). Silence and speech—the wise know when to speak and when to be still; the fool speaks at all times. Love and hate—not moral relativism but the recognition that covenant love requires appropriate rejection of evil (Ps 97:10; Rom 12:9). War and peace—the final and most encompassing pair: God governs the timing of conflict and resolution in national life. The poem ends where human life is most catastrophically disrupted—war—as if to say: even this is under God's sovereign appointment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–22 — Eternity, Justice, and What Remains
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The poem of times raises the same question as the rest of the book: what gain does the worker have? Qohelet's answer deepens: God has made everything beautiful in its time, but he has also placed eternity in the human heart so that people cannot fully grasp what God is doing. The proper response is the enjoyment of present gifts, trust in God's enduring purposes, and the acknowledgment that God will judge injustice. The chapter ends with the recognition that humans share mortality with the animals—which is not final cynicism but a preparation for the fear of God.
verseByVerse.theology: The phrase 'eternity in man's heart' (v. 11) is one of the most profound anthropological statements in Scripture. The Hebrew olam can mean eternity, the distant future, or a vast span of time. God has wired into every human being a longing for permanence, for the enduring, for what transcends the cycles of hebel. This is not a curse but a design: the longing for eternity is what makes us responsive to the gospel, which offers the eternal life our hearts were built to desire. Augustine's restless heart—'our hearts are restless until they find their rest in thee'—is a commentary on this verse.
verseByVerse.examples: Verses 16–22 introduce the problem of injustice that will recur in chapters 4, 5, and 8. The Preacher's response is not denial ('injustice does not exist') or despair ('injustice cannot be remedied') but eschatological faith: 'God will judge the righteous and the wicked' (v. 17). The timing of this judgment is God's to determine, not ours to demand. In the meantime, the proper human posture is the enjoyment of present gifts while trusting God's ultimate governance.

verseByVerse.quote: What gain has the worker from his toil? I have seen the business that God has given to the children of man to be busy with. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The poem of times prompts the same question as 1:3—what does the worker gain? But the context now is different: if the times are God's, then the work is also God's business, not merely human striving. 'The business that God has given'—the word inyan (business, preoccupation) appears again. God has given humans a task that is genuinely demanding and genuinely meaningful, even if the gain is not what they expect. The question is not answered with despair but with observation: God has given this work, and it is woven into the fabric of creation.

verseByVerse.quote: He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also put eternity into man's heart, yet so that he cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end. I perceived that there is nothing better for them than to be joyful and to do good as long as they live. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Everything beautiful in its time'—God's governance produces beauty when the right things happen at the right moments. But the beauty is God's achievement, not a product of human control. 'Eternity in man's heart'—this is the theological explanation for why nothing satisfies: God has built into every human a longing for the permanent that no finite thing can fill. This longing is not a malfunction but a design feature pointing toward God himself. The practical response: 'be joyful and do good.' These are not escapism but faithful responses to a world where God is sovereign and good is possible even within the limits of hebel.

verseByVerse.quote: Also that everyone should eat and drink and take pleasure in his toil—this is God's gift to man. I perceived that whatever God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it. God has done it, so that people fear before him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'God's gift'—the carpe diem refrain again, now explicitly framed as gift. Enjoyment is not grasped; it is received. 'Whatever God does endures forever'—in contrast to the cycles of hebel, God's actions are permanent, complete, and beyond human amendment. 'Nothing can be added to it, nor anything taken from it'—God's decree is immutable. The purpose of this immutability is theological: 'so that people fear before him.' The stability of God's governance, contrasted with the instability of all human construction, is designed to produce the fear of God—which is Ecclesiastes' ultimate destination (12:13).

verseByVerse.quote: What is, already has been; what is to be, already has been; and God seeks what has been driven away. Moreover, I saw under the sun that in the place of justice, even there was wickedness, and in the place of righteousness, even there was wickedness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'God seeks what has been driven away'—a remarkable phrase suggesting God's providential recovery: what the cycles of time have pushed aside, God pursues and reclaims. Then the observation of injustice: the court system (place of justice) corrupted by wickedness; the religious institution (place of righteousness) infiltrated by evil. This is not cynicism but accurate observation. The institutions humans build to achieve justice are themselves fallen. The remedy cannot come from within the system—it must come from above it.

verseByVerse.quote: I said in my heart, 'God will judge the righteous and the wicked, for there is a time for every matter and for every work.' I said in my heart with regard to the children of man that God is testing them that they may see that they themselves are but beasts. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'God will judge the righteous and the wicked'—eschatological faith answering the problem of injustice. The judgment may not come in the timeframe we expect, but it will come: God has appointed a time for every matter, including judgment. Then the sobering observation about mortality: God is testing humans through their shared mortality with the animals, 'that they may see that they themselves are but beasts.' The point is not that humans are only animals but that from the horizontal perspective—without the fear of God, without resurrection hope—human death looks indistinguishable from animal death.

verseByVerse.quote: For what happens to the children of man and what happens to the beasts is the same; as one dies, so dies the other. They all have the same breath, and man has no advantage over the beasts, for all is vanity. All go to one place. All are from the dust, and to dust all return. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'From the dust, and to dust all return'—Genesis 3:19 applied to the horizontal observation. This is not Qohelet's final word on human destiny (cf. 12:7: 'the spirit returns to God who gave it'), but it is the perspective from under the sun: bodily death is the universal leveler. The materialist must face this without hope. The believer faces it knowing that the dust is not the whole story—that the God who breathed life into dust at creation will breathe it again at resurrection. Ecclesiastes holds the tension without resolving it prematurely.

verseByVerse.quote: Who knows whether the spirit of man goes up and the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth? So I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his work, for that is his lot. Who can bring him to see what will be after him? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Who knows'—Qohelet raises the question of the spirit's destiny without answering it definitively (at this point). The uncertainty is deliberate: under the sun, with no special revelation, the question is unanswerable. The practical response is not paralysis but the carpe diem refrain: rejoice in your work, for that is your lot. 'Who can bring him to see what will be after him?'—no human can. But God can, and has—through resurrection and final judgment. Ecclesiastes is a preparation for gospel: the questions it raises can only be answered by the one who conquered death.

4.title: Ecclesiastes 4 — Oppression, Solitude, and the Better Way of Companionship

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Social Fabric of Vanity: Oppression, Ambition, and the Gift of Community
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 4 surveys four social realities: oppression without comfort (vv. 1–3), competitive toil driven by envy (vv. 4–6), isolated accumulation without purpose (vv. 7–8), and the dangerous instability of political favor (vv. 13–16). Against the darkness of isolation and ambition, the centerpiece of the chapter is the famous poem on companionship (vv. 9–12): two are better than one. The chapter is not a social manifesto but a wisdom observation—life is not meant to be lived alone, and the structures humans build for power and wealth are more fragile than they appear.
verseByVerse.theology: The oppression passage (vv. 1–3) is one of the most emotionally raw in Ecclesiastes: Qohelet weeps for the oppressed. The repetition—'they had no one to comfort them'—is a deliberate, painful echo. This is not detached analysis but pastoral grief. The social critique continues through the chapter: competitive ambition (v. 4), pathological overwork (vv. 7–8), political instability (vv. 13–16). Each observation confirms that structures built by fallen humans tend toward isolation, exploitation, and eventually collapse. The remedy is not more structure but the fear of God and the gift of true companionship.
verseByVerse.examples: The 'threefold cord not quickly broken' (v. 12) has been applied to Christian marriage (two persons united before God, the third strand). More broadly it describes the principle of covenantal community: individual vulnerability is addressed not by individual strength but by mutual commitment. Keller: 'The answer to the oppression and isolation of fallen social structures is not better political organization but the community that the gospel creates—bound together not by utility but by the love of the one who was abandoned so that no one need be alone.'

verseByVerse.quote: Again I saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun. And behold, the tears of the oppressed, and they had no one to comfort them! On the side of their oppressors there was power, and there was no one to comfort them. And I thought the dead who are already dead more fortunate than the living who are still alive. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The tears, the oppressors' power, the absence of a comforter—twice stated in a single verse. The repetition of 'no one to comfort them' is the theological indictment: the created order, left to human management, produces suffering without relief. Qohelet does not rush past the tears; he sits with them. His conclusion that the dead are more fortunate than the suffering living is not suicide advocacy but the raw articulation of grief in the face of unrelieved injustice. The Psalms contain the same: 'It would have been better had I never been born' (Ps 22, by implication). Honest lament is not faithlessness.

verseByVerse.quote: But better than both is he who has not yet been and has not seen the evil deeds that are done under the sun. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The not-yet-born are spared the sight of oppression—a thought that echoes Job (3:11–13) and Jeremiah (20:14–18). This is not nihilism but the extreme expression of grief: the world's evil is so pervasive that non-existence seems preferable to witnessing it. Qohelet allows the thought to stand without qualification—he is recording the emotional logic of anguish, not prescribing a worldview. The redemptive response to this passage is not a quick theological correction but the incarnation: God himself entered the world of tears, and the comforter who was absent from the oppressed has now come in the person of the Holy Spirit (John 14:16–17).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I saw that all toil and all skill in work come from a man's envy of his neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind. The fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The engine of achievement is competitive envy—'a man's envy of his neighbor.' This is a sobering diagnostic: much of what drives human productivity is not love of the work, not service of others, not glory of God, but the desire to surpass someone else. The ambition that builds civilizations is fueled by the sin that fractured Eden. Yet the opposite is not better: 'the fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh.' Sloth is self-destructive. The Preacher is not counseling laziness; he is exposing the false dichotomy between frantic achievement and passive inaction, preparing for the alternative: verse 6.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is a handful of quietness than two hands full of toil and a striving after wind. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A handful of quietness'—the image is precise. One hand holds a modest portion; two hands hold the maximum possible. But the double portion comes at the cost of ceaseless striving and wind-chasing. The single portion, held with contentment and rest, is more valuable than the double portion won through envy-driven overwork. This is the wisdom of contentment that Paul echoes: 'I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content' (Phil 4:11). Contentment is not a natural disposition; it is learned wisdom, and Ecclesiastes is one of the great teachers.

verseByVerse.quote: Again, I saw vanity under the sun: one person who has no other, either son or brother, yet there is no end to all his toil, and his eyes are never satisfied with riches, so that he never asks, 'For whom am I toiling and depriving myself of pleasure?' This also is vanity and an unhappy business. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The solitary accumulator—no family, no partner, no heir—yet unable to stop. 'His eyes are never satisfied with riches'—the appetite of wealth is infinite, as 5:10 will confirm. The haunting question he never asks: 'For whom am I toiling?' He has no answer, and so he never asks. The tragedy is the unexamined life: he works without purpose, accumulates without beneficiary, deprives himself of pleasure for no reason he can articulate. Kidner: 'This is the portrait of a man who has let his industry become his identity—he cannot stop because stopping would force him to confront the emptiness.'

verseByVerse.quote: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil'—the proverb is practical before it is romantic. The reward of shared labor is greater because the resources (skills, energy, encouragement) are multiplied while the risks (failure, injury, discouragement) are distributed. 'If they fall, one will lift up his fellow'—the image of two travelers supporting each other on rough ground. 'Woe to him who is alone when he falls'—the loneliness of the solitary person in crisis is real and dangerous. The community of God's people is designed for exactly this: bearing one another's burdens (Gal 6:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Again, if two lie together, they keep warm, but how can one keep warm alone? And though a man might prevail against one who is alone, two will withstand him—a threefold cord is not quickly broken. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Warmth and protection: the physical images of companionship's benefits. Shared body heat against the cold night—survival through proximity. Two can resist an attacker that would overcome one. Then the famous proverb: 'a threefold cord is not quickly broken.' The addition of a third strand—understood in the Christian tradition as God, the third party in any covenant relationship—increases resilience exponentially. The cord metaphor is exact: individual strands are weak; braided together they become a rope. Community is not an optional enhancement to the Christian life; it is structural.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knows how to take advice. For he came out of prison to reign, even though in his own kingdom he had been born poor. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The political proverb: wisdom and poverty trump age and power when the powerful person has stopped listening. The old king who cannot receive counsel is more dangerous than the young man who came from prison. The young man's rise from poverty and imprisonment to the throne is a pattern Qohelet's audience would recognize—and it echoes Joseph's story unmistakably (Gen 41:14). Wisdom, not status, is what qualifies a person for genuine leadership. But the next verses show that even this wisdom-grounded success is unstable.

verseByVerse.quote: I saw all the living who move about under the sun, as well as that youth who was to stand in the king's place. There was no end of all the people, all of whom he led. Yet those who come later will not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and a striving after wind. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Even the wise youth who rises to power will be forgotten. The crowds who celebrated his rise will be replaced by a generation that never knew him, and that generation will not be grateful. Political fame is among the most transient of all human achievements. The crowds are fickle; history is short-memoried; the next leader displaces the last. Sproul: 'Every earthly king is temporary; every political savior is eventually replaced. The only reign that does not end in forgetting is the reign of the one whose kingdom has no end—Daniel 7:14.'

5.title: Ecclesiastes 5 — Fear of God, Rash Vows, and the Gift of Contentment

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Approaching God: Reverence, Listening, and the Weight of Vows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After surveying human social failures, Qohelet turns to the most important relationship: the human person before God. The counsel here is counter-cultural in every era: approach God to listen, not to speak; say little, not much; pay what you vow or do not vow at all. The fear of God is the controlling attitude—God is in heaven and you are on earth; let your words reflect that asymmetry.
verseByVerse.theology: The Temple approach (v. 1) begins the section. 'House of God' refers to the Jerusalem Temple, the place of sacrifice and prayer. Qohelet's concern is not with the mechanics of sacrifice but with the heart posture that accompanies it: are you coming to listen or to perform? The 'sacrifice of fools' is impressive in external appearance but empty in spiritual substance—it substitutes religious busyness for genuine attentiveness to God. The section culminates in v. 7: 'fear God.' This is not a pious add-on but the structural solution to all the vanity surveyed in chapters 1–4.
verseByVerse.examples: The vow passage (vv. 4–6) reflects Deuteronomy 23:21–23 and Numbers 30. Vows were solemn covenant commitments, binding before God. Qohelet's counsel—pay promptly, or better not vow at all—is practical wisdom rooted in the fear of God. The person who makes vows carelessly is treating God as a contract partner to be negotiated with rather than a sovereign to be honored. Kidner: 'The lightness with which we treat our promises to God reflects the lightness with which we conceive of God himself.'

verseByVerse.quote: Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. To draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools, for they do not know that they are doing evil. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Guard your steps'—the image of deliberate, careful approach. Not rushing into God's presence with a shopping list but coming with intentional readiness to receive. 'To draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools'—the contrast is between attentiveness and performance. The sacrifice of fools is not a different animal but a different orientation: they offer with mouths full of words and hearts empty of attention. They 'do not know that they are doing evil'—religious self-deception is among the most dangerous conditions, because it feels righteous while it offends God. Samuel said it plainly: 'to obey is better than sacrifice' (1 Sam 15:22).

verseByVerse.quote: Be not rash with your mouth, nor let your heart be hasty to utter a word before God, for God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few. For a dream comes with much business, and a fool's voice with many words. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'God is in heaven and you are on earth'—the most concise statement of divine transcendence in Ecclesiastes. The consequence is not silence but restraint: 'let your words be few.' Prayer is not measured by volume but by reality; many words do not increase the likelihood of being heard (cf. Matt 6:7). The parallel: dreams come from mental busyness (many thoughts, much anxiety), and a fool's prayer comes from verbal busyness (many words, little thought). Kidner: 'The fool mistakes fluency for sincerity and length for devotion.' Jesus's model prayer is twenty-five words in its core petitions—an enacted commentary on this verse.

verseByVerse.quote: When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay what you vow. It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Do not delay paying it'—God takes vows seriously even when we later regret making them. 'He has no pleasure in fools'—the fool makes vows in moments of crisis or enthusiasm and then quietly forgets them. The remedy is either immediate payment or non-vowing. 'Better not to vow than to vow and not pay'—this is not discouraging vows but demanding that they be made with full seriousness. Jephthah's tragedy (Judg 11) and Ananias and Sapphira's death (Acts 5) are both cautionary texts on the same theme: God is not lenient about broken commitments made in his name.

verseByVerse.quote: Let not your mouth lead you into sin, and do not say before the messenger that it was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands? For when dreams increase and words grow many, there is vanity; but God is the one you must fear. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Do not say before the messenger that it was a mistake'—the 'messenger' (malak) may refer to the temple priest who oversaw vow fulfillment. The excuse 'it was a mistake' is a post-hoc rationalization for a vow one no longer wants to keep. God will not be satisfied by this rationalization; he may destroy what you have built. The section closes with the key command: 'fear God.' This is not fear as terror but fear as the foundational orientation of the creature before the Creator—reverence, awe, and obedience. All the vow-breaking, all the rash speech, all the religious performance flows from insufficient fear of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–20 — Wealth's Vanity and the Gift of Contentment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of chapter 5 returns to economic realities: the corruption of bureaucratic systems (vv. 8–9), the insatiability of wealth (vv. 10–12), the tragedy of riches lost and naked departure from life (vv. 13–17), and the positive conclusion: the gift of enjoyment from God's hand (vv. 18–20). The section is not anti-wealth but anti-idolatry: wealth fails as a source of satisfaction, security, and ultimate meaning.
verseByVerse.theology: The structural insight of the section is that wealth's failure is diagnostic, not accidental. God has arranged the world so that finite riches cannot satisfy infinite desire (v. 10), that accumulated wealth requires more people to consume it (v. 11), that rich anxiety prevents sleep while poverty enables it (v. 12), and that death returns everyone to nakedness (v. 15). These are not random inconveniences but pedagogical features: the dissatisfaction of wealth is designed to drive the person toward the true satisfaction that only God provides.
verseByVerse.examples: The carpe diem conclusion of vv. 18–20 is the most developed in Ecclesiastes so far: God gives wealth, possessions, and power to enjoy—and this enjoyment is itself a gift. The person who enjoys their work without demanding that it provide ultimate meaning has found the key to Ecclesiastes: receive the gift without making the gift your god. Keller: 'The person who is grateful for a meal because God gave it enjoys it more than the person who eats it as a right—because gratitude adds the dimension of relationship to the experience of eating.'

verseByVerse.quote: If you see in a province the oppression of the poor and the violation of justice and righteousness, do not be amazed at the matter, for the high official is watched by a higher, and there are yet higher ones over them. But this is gain for a land in every way: a king committed to cultivated fields. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Do not be amazed at the matter'—systemic injustice is not a surprise; it is the predictable product of hierarchical bureaucracy where each level exploits the level below. The Preacher is not counseling passivity but clear-eyed realism: expecting a fallen bureaucracy to deliver perfect justice is naive. 'A king committed to cultivated fields'—the best political situation is a king who grounds his economy in agricultural productivity rather than in extractive taxation of the poor. Genuine governance serves the land and the people who work it; exploitative governance extracts from both.

verseByVerse.quote: He who loves money will not be satisfied with money, nor he who loves wealth with his income; this also is vanity. When goods increase, they increase who eat them, and what advantage has their owner but to see them with his eyes? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He who loves money will not be satisfied with money'—one of the most empirically verifiable statements in Scripture. Wealth does not satisfy the desire for wealth; it escalates it. This is not a biblical peculiarity but a feature of all addictive structures: the dose required for the same effect keeps increasing. 'When goods increase, they increase who eat them'—the wealthy person discovers that more wealth requires more staff, more maintenance, more security, and more tax—leaving the owner with the same net satisfaction but greater complexity. The advantage of great wealth is the visual pleasure of seeing it: almost nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Sweet is the sleep of a laborer, whether he eats little or much, but the full stomach of the rich will not let him sleep. There is a grievous evil that I have seen under the sun: riches were kept by their owner to his hurt. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Sweet is the sleep of a laborer'—one of the most practical observations in Ecclesiastes. Physical exhaustion from honest work produces restful sleep regardless of the size of the meal. The wealthy person, whose stomach is full and whose mind is preoccupied with preserving and multiplying wealth, cannot sleep. Anxiety is the tax that great wealth imposes on its owners. 'Riches kept to their owner's hurt'—this is the grievous evil: wealth hoarded rather than given or enjoyed, generating anxiety, relational damage, and ultimately loss.

verseByVerse.quote: And those riches were lost in a bad venture. And he is father of a son, but he has nothing in his hand. As he came from his mother's womb he shall go again, naked as he came, and shall take nothing for his toil that he may carry in his hand. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The riches are lost—bad investment, economic collapse, catastrophe. The father who counted on his wealth to provide for his son has nothing to give. Then the final stripping: at death, as at birth, the person leaves with nothing. 'Naked as he came'—the radical equality of death. Job knew this: 'Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return' (Job 1:21). Paul knew this: 'We brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out' (1 Tim 6:7). The only wealth that survives death is what is deposited in the kingdom of God.

verseByVerse.quote: This also is a grievous evil: just as he came, so shall he go, and what gain is there to him who toils for the wind? Moreover, all his days he eats in darkness and suffers much vexation and sickness and anger. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Toils for the wind'—another iteration of the striving-after-wind image. The wealth accumulator's life is not merely ultimately unrewarding; it is immediately painful: eating in darkness (without the joy of good company and proper nourishment), suffering vexation, sickness, and anger. These are the interior companions of the person who has made wealth their god—the anxiety, resentment, and relational isolation that accompany obsessive accumulation. The full picture of the wealthy life Qohelet has observed is not enviable from the inside.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, what I have seen to be good and fitting is to eat and drink and find enjoyment in all the toil with which one toils under the sun the few days of his life that God has given him, for this is his lot. Everyone also to whom God has given wealth and possessions and power to enjoy them, and to accept his lot and rejoice in his toil—this is the gift of God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'This is the gift of God'—the carpe diem refrain now with explicit theological grounding. Wealth itself is not condemned; the inability to enjoy wealth is the problem. God gives both wealth and the power to enjoy it—and both are gifts, not achievements. The person who has wealth but lacks the power to enjoy it (cf. 6:1–2) is in a worse position than the person who has little but enjoys it fully. 'Accept his lot'—the Hebrew word for lot (helqo) is the same as inheritance or portion: what God assigns is to be received with gratitude rather than resented as insufficient.

verseByVerse.quote: For he will not much remember the days of his life because God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'God keeps him occupied with joy'—the person who receives their lot with gratitude is so filled with the present gift that the anxious preoccupation with past and future fades. This is not forgetfulness but the liberation of presence: living fully in the moment God has given. Kidner: 'Joy that comes from God's hand is not distracted by the past or paralyzed by the future—it is present to the present.' This is the psychological fruit of the fear of God: not constant elation but a deep, received contentment that anchors the heart in what God is giving today.

6.title: Ecclesiastes 6 — The Unsatisfied Soul: When Blessing Fails to Bless

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Grievous Evil of Unenjoyed Abundance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 6 explores a specific and common tragedy: the person who has everything God could give—wealth, possessions, honor, long life, many children—yet lacks the capacity to enjoy any of it. The chapter pushes the theological point that enjoyment is itself a gift of God that cannot be manufactured by human effort or accumulated by human achievement. A stillborn child who knows nothing is, Qohelet argues, better off than this unenjoyed life. The chapter ends with a pair of questions that close the first half of the book: who knows what is good for man in his few vain days? And who can tell what will come after?
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter is theologically crucial because it closes the circle: chapter 2 showed that pleasure-seeking fails, chapter 5 showed that wealth-hoarding fails, and chapter 6 shows that even the combination of wealth, honor, and longevity fails when God does not give the power to enjoy. The failure is not in the gifts but in the receiver's orientation. The fear of God produces the capacity for enjoyment (5:18–20); the absence of that orientation leaves even the most blessed person unsatisfied. This is the doctrine of total depravity applied to the gift of enjoyment: even this good thing is corrupted by the fallen orientation of the heart.
verseByVerse.examples: The section's climax is the question of v. 12: 'For who knows what is good for man while he lives the few days of his vain life?' This question prepares for the wisdom section of chapters 7–11, where Qohelet will answer it with a series of 'better than' proverbs. The answer is not a program for achieving the good life but an orientation—the fear of God—that receives whatever life brings as gift and governance.

verseByVerse.quote: There is an evil that I have seen under the sun, and it lies heavy on mankind: a man to whom God gives wealth, possessions, and honor, so that he lacks nothing of all that he desires, yet God does not give him power to enjoy them, but a stranger enjoys them. This is vanity; it is a grievous evil. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The gifts are divine: God gives the wealth, possessions, and honor. The deprivation is also divine: God does not give the power to enjoy them. This is a startling observation—not that wealth fails to satisfy (chapter 2 established that), but that even the perfectly provisioned person can be left without the capacity for enjoyment. The 'stranger' who enjoys what the original recipient cannot is a figure of judgment: the one who received the gifts without gratitude loses even the possibility of enjoyment. Keller: 'The inability to enjoy is the most underrated form of poverty.'

verseByVerse.quote: If a man fathers a hundred children and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not satisfied with life's good things, and he also has no burial, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he. For it comes in vanity and goes in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: One hundred children, many years of life—the maximum of ancient blessings. But 'his soul is not satisfied with life's good things'—the inner orientation defeats the outer abundance. And 'no burial'—the final indignity, to die without the honor of a proper funeral. Against this life, Qohelet compares the stillborn: it comes in vanity (without achievement), goes in darkness (without recognition), its name is covered (forgotten immediately). Yet the stillborn finds rest. The logic is painful: a life of maximum external blessing without internal satisfaction is worse than no life at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, it has not seen the sun or known anything, yet it finds rest rather than he. Even though he should live a thousand years twice over, yet enjoy no good—do not all go to the one place? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'It finds rest rather than he'—the stillborn is at rest; the unsatisfied man, despite all his blessings, finds no rest. Two thousand years of unenjoyed life is worse than a moment of existence. Death is the great leveler: 'do not all go to the one place?' Whether rich or poor, whether satisfied or unsatisfied, whether five years or two thousand, all arrive at the same destination. The length of the unenjoyed life is not a compensation; it is an amplification of the misery. This is the theological case against treating long life as an unconditional blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied. For what advantage has the wise man over the fool? And what does the poor man have who knows how to conduct himself before the living? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'All the toil of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied'—the biological engine of labor is the mouth (hunger), yet the mouth is never permanently full. This is the structural insatiability of human desire: we labor to eat, eat to work, work to eat again. 'What advantage has the wise man over the fool?'—the leveling question again. The wise man and the fool both eat, both desire more, both die. The social skill of the poor man ('conducting himself before the living') does not ultimately improve his position relative to the rich. The horizontal perspective consistently collapses all distinctions before death.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the appetite: this also is vanity and a striving after wind. Whatever has come to be has already been named, and it is known what man is, and that he is not able to dispute with one stronger than he. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the appetite'—better the actual good in front of you than the imagined good you are always pursuing. The wandering appetite (the Hebrew images a soul that walks) is always somewhere else, always dissatisfied with the present. The present good seen by the eyes is the actual gift; the imagined better good is the trap. 'Man is not able to dispute with one stronger than he'—God determines what comes to be. The human person who disputes with God's ordering of events is engaged in a losing argument. Wisdom begins with receiving what God gives.

verseByVerse.quote: The more words, the more vanity, and what is the advantage to man? For who knows what is good for man while he lives the few days of his vain life, which he passes like a shadow? For who can tell man what will be after him under the sun? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The more words, the more vanity'—a fitting close to a chapter that has exposed the inadequacy of human categories and calculations. More words do not solve the problem of unenjoyed abundance; they merely add to the hebel. The final double question closes the first half of the book: who knows what is good for man? And who can tell what comes after? These questions are not rhetorical despair but the opening of the investigation that chapters 7–12 will pursue. The partial answer comes in 12:13: fear God and keep his commandments. The full answer comes in the resurrection of the one who said, 'I am the resurrection and the life.'

7.title: Ecclesiastes 7 — Better-Than Proverbs: The Wisdom of Facing Reality

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Wisdom for the Realist: Better-Than Proverbs and the Search for Understanding
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 7 is the pivot of the book. The first half of Ecclesiastes (1–6) diagnosed the problem; chapters 7–12 begin developing the response. The chapter opens with a series of 'better than' proverbs that deliberately subvert conventional wisdom: the day of death is better than the day of birth; the house of mourning is better than the house of feasting; the rebuke of the wise is better than the song of fools. These are not counsel to morbidity but to realism—the person who can face death, sorrow, and correction has a firmer grip on reality than the person who seeks only comfort.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter's central section (vv. 13–22) counsels balance in the face of life's contradictions: prosperity and adversity both come from God; neither extreme righteousness nor extreme wickedness is prescribed; the fear of God navigates through both. Then vv. 23–29 record Qohelet's exhausting search for wisdom—finding it elusive—and his final conclusion: God made man upright, but humans have sought out many schemes. The chapter ends not with despair but with the diagnosis of the fall: the problem is not creation but corruption.
verseByVerse.examples: The 'better than' proverbs of vv. 1–14 are a masterclass in the theology of suffering and limitation. Keller: 'Ecclesiastes 7 is the wisdom book's equivalent of Romans 5:3—we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance. Qohelet's point is not that mourning is enjoyable but that it is honest and formative in a way that false mirth cannot be.' The house of mourning teaches what the house of feasting cannot: the truth about human finitude, and therefore the proper orientation toward God and neighbor.

verseByVerse.quote: A good name is better than precious ointment, and the day of death than the day of birth. It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, for this is the end of all mankind, and the living will lay it to heart. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A good name is better than precious ointment'—the Hebrew pun: shem (name) and shemen (ointment) sound alike. Character outlasts cosmetics. Then the provocative proverb: 'the day of death than the day of birth.' Not because death is pleasant but because death brings clarity: it reveals what a life was actually worth, what relationships were genuine, what investments lasted. 'The house of mourning'—at a funeral, human beings face the truth about themselves and each other with unusual honesty. The feasting house offers pleasure but not wisdom. The living 'lay it to heart': mortality is the great teacher of priorities.

verseByVerse.quote: Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad. The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'By sadness of face the heart is made glad'—the paradox is exact: the external expression of grief produces an internal deepening of character that eventually issues in genuine gladness, not the surface gladness of the feasting house but the settled peace of a person who has faced reality. The wise person's heart is in the house of mourning—not morbidly, but because that is where truth is spoken and received. The fool's heart is in the house of mirth—not because mirth is bad but because the fool uses mirth as a substitute for reality rather than a fruit of it. Kidner: 'Joy built on avoidance is not joy but anesthesia.'

verseByVerse.quote: It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise than to hear the song of fools. For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of fools; this also is vanity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Rebuke of the wise'—painful to receive, productive in effect. 'Song of fools'—pleasant to hear, useless for formation. The image of thorns crackling under a pot is precise: thorns burn quickly and noisily, producing heat briefly and then ash. The laughter of fools is just such a blaze—impressive for a moment, useful for nothing. The wise person chooses the rebuke because they are oriented toward growth rather than comfort. Proverbs says the same: 'Better is open rebuke than hidden love' (27:5). Christian fellowship requires the courage to speak and the humility to receive correction.

verseByVerse.quote: Surely oppression drives the wise into madness, and a bribe corrupts the heart. Better is the end of a thing than its beginning, and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Oppression drives the wise into madness'—even wisdom is not immune to the distorting effects of sustained injustice. A bribe corrupts the heart of the just judge: no one is so wise that they are beyond corruption if the pressure is sustained. Then the proverbs of patience: the end of a thing is better than the beginning because the end reveals what the beginning promised. A building at completion is greater than a foundation. A life at its end is more fully known than at its beginning. 'Patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit'—patience is the fruit of trust in God's timing; pride insists on its own schedule.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not quick in your spirit to become angry, for anger lodges in the heart of fools. Say not, 'Why were the former days better than these?' for it is not from wisdom that you ask this. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Anger lodges in the heart of fools'—anger that dwells, that refuses to move on, that makes itself at home in the soul is the mark of foolishness. This is not a prohibition of righteous anger (Eph 4:26 permits anger without sin) but of the resentful, self-pitying anger that festers. 'Why were the former days better than these?'—nostalgia is not wisdom. The question assumes that the past was objectively better, which is rarely accurate and always unproductive. The wise person engages the present rather than mourning an idealized past. Kidner: 'Nostalgia is the mood of people who have given up on the present.'

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom is good with an inheritance, an advantage to those who see the sun. For the protection of wisdom is like the protection of money, and the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of him who has it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Wisdom and money are compared not to equate them but to show wisdom's superiority: money protects (through resources, influence, access), and wisdom also protects—but wisdom preserves life itself, not merely comfort. 'An inheritance' plus wisdom is the ideal: the material resource that enables wisdom's exercise. But wisdom without money still preserves; money without wisdom does not. The book of Proverbs makes the same comparison: wisdom is 'more precious than jewels' (Prov 8:11). The protection of wisdom is interior: it shapes the decisions that money cannot buy.

verseByVerse.quote: Consider the work of God: who can make straight what he has made crooked? In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider: God has made the one as well as the other, so that man may not find out anything that will be after him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Who can make straight what he has made crooked?'—God's governance includes the difficult, the painful, the frustrating. What he has bent to his purposes cannot be unbent by human ingenuity. This is not fatalism but realism: accepting what God has ordered rather than expending energy raging against his appointments. 'God has made the one as well as the other'—both prosperity and adversity are from his hand. The purpose of their alternation is to prevent human self-sufficiency: if prosperity were constant, we would trust ourselves; if adversity were constant, we would despair. The mixture keeps us dependent on God.

verseByVerse.quote: In my vain life I have seen everything. There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man who prolongs his life in his evildoing. Be not overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you destroy yourself? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Qohelet has seen the retribution principle fail: righteous people die young; wicked people live long. This observation parallels Psalm 73. The counsel against 'overly righteous' behavior is not a counsel to sin but a warning against a particular kind of piety that demands God conform to a retribution formula—performing righteousness as a technology for securing long life. When the technology fails (as it does), such people are devastated. The person who performs righteousness to control God will 'destroy themselves' when God does not comply with the expected outcome.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not overly wicked, neither be a fool. Why should you die before your time? It is good that you should take hold of this, and from that withhold not your hand, for the one who fears God shall come out from both of them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Be not overly wicked'—this is not permission for moderate wickedness but a warning against the presumption that God's patience is infinite. The person who sins carelessly, counting on the delay of judgment, may 'die before their time'—face the consequences of wickedness before they expect to. 'The one who fears God shall come out from both of them'—the fear of God is the navigation through the twin errors of self-righteous religion and careless wickedness. The God-fearer is neither a legalist who demands God's compliance nor a libertine who presumes on God's patience.

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom gives strength to the wise man more than ten rulers who are in a city. Surely there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Wisdom gives strength to the wise man more than ten rulers'—wisdom's power exceeds political power. The wisdom that reads situations correctly, that speaks at the right moment, that navigates conflict without escalation is more valuable than the resources of a city's entire leadership. Then the universal qualification: 'there is not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins.' This is one of the Bible's most compact statements of total depravity. It closes the argument against the 'overly righteous' person: no one is so righteous that they have not sinned. The ground of confidence before God cannot be human righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not take to heart all the things that people say, lest you hear your servant cursing you. For your heart knows that many times you yourself have cursed others. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Practical wisdom on reputation sensitivity: do not monitor everything said about you.
